title: Delete Nodes And Return Forest
spaceBreakdown:
- unordered_set<int> toDel: up to k entries (k = to_delete.size()) → O(k)
- recursion call stack: worst case skewed tree depth n → O(n)
- not counted: input tree (modified in place), returned vector
approach: Use post-order DFS carrying a boolean indicating whether the parent was deleted. A hash set provides O(1) deletion checks. When a node is deleted, return nullptr so the parent nulls its child pointer; the deleted node's children are recursed first with parentDeleted=true, so any surviving child is added to the result. The initial call uses parentDeleted=true so the root becomes a forest root if it survives.
hints: When a node is removed, its children lose their connection to everything above them - what does each surviving child become, and what must you know about a node's parent to decide whether to collect it as a new root?

Post-order DFS carrying a boolean "parent was deleted"; use a hash set for O(1) deletion checks. In Example 1, deleting node 3 makes children 6 and 7 new roots, so dfs adds them when it visits them with parentDeleted = true.

```
dfs(node, parentDeleted):
    if node is null: return null
    deleted = node.val in deleteSet
    node.left  = dfs(node.left,  deleted)
    node.right = dfs(node.right, deleted)
    if deleted: return null
    if parentDeleted: append node to result
    return node
```

**Single node deleted** - root is the only node and is in to_delete
`Input: root = [1], to_delete = [1]` → `Expected: []`
⚠️ Bug: unconditionally adding root to result before calling dfs → returns `[[1]]`

**No deletions** - to_delete is empty, entire tree survives
`Input: root = [1,2,3], to_delete = []` → `Expected: [[1,2,3]]`
⚠️ Bug: calling dfs(root, false) instead of dfs(root, true) → root never added, returns `[]`

**Skewed tree, middle deleted** - right-skewed list, middle node deleted
`Input: root = [1,null,2,null,3], to_delete = [2]` → `Expected: [[1],[3]]`
⚠️ Bug: not assigning dfs return value to node->right → deleted node 2 stays attached, returns `[[1,null,2,null,3]]`

**All nodes deleted** - every node in to_delete
`Input: root = [1,2,3], to_delete = [1,2,3]` → `Expected: []`
⚠️ Bug: checking parentDeleted before deleted (wrong order) → adds all three nodes, returns `[[1],[2],[3]]`

followUps.q: What if deletion values arrive one at a time online, and you must report the forest after each deletion?
followUps.a: Store parent pointers for every node and maintain a set of current roots. On each deletion, detach the node from its parent, add its non-deleted children to the root set, and remove the node from the root set if present. Each deletion is O(1) amortized; total O(n + q) time and O(n) space, where q is the number of queries.

followUps.q: What if node values are not distinct - how do you delete specific nodes?
followUps.a: Key the deletion set on node pointers instead of values. The DFS structure stays identical; only the lookup changes from a value-based set to a pointer-based set. Time and space complexity remain O(n).

followUps.q: What if after deletions, you must support queries asking whether two surviving nodes are in the same tree?
followUps.a: After building the forest with the same DFS, run union-find over all surviving nodes: union each node with its surviving children. Preprocessing is O(n α(n)) time and O(n) space; each query is O(α(n)) amortized.
